body: **Summary:** EMS companies assemble electronics for brand owners: mobiles, TVs, IT hardware and wearables, plus industrial, auto and defence boards. Profit is a thin conversion margin (2–4% EBITDA for mobile assembly, 8–15% for industrial/auto boards) on huge pass-through revenue, so RoCE comes from asset turns and working-capital speed. PLI incentives have been a material share of profit. Backward integration (displays, camera modules, PCBs under ECMS) offers higher margins. Key metrics: revenue growth by segment, EBITDA margin and absolute EBITDA, RoCE, net working capital days, customer concentration, PLI income as a share of EBITDA, export share, value addition %, and capex for component plants. Cycle drivers: smartphone demand and brand outsourcing decisions (Apple, Samsung, Chinese brands seeking JV partners), PLI scheme tenure (mobile PLI ended FY26), ECMS component incentives, US tariffs and China+1, and GST and tariff duty structure. Lead indicators: MeitY production and export data, ICEA mobile export data, Commerce Ministry HS 8517 exports, ECMS approval notifications, client announcements. Winners (Dixon over 2018–25) made early bets on mobile PLI, ran a capital-light, high asset-turn model and moved up into components. Losers suffered customer loss (single-client concentration) or working-capital blow-outs. Kaynes in 2025 showed how accounting-disclosure concerns can hit a high-multiple stock. Valuation: P/E 60–120x at the 2024–25 peak. Nov 2026: Dixon's Q2 FY27 revenue rose sharply (+35% to +47%; sources differ), but operating margin fell to 2.7% from 3.8% as mobile PLI ended, PAT fell 45% on lower other income, and ₹1,110 cr of PLI receivables are outstanding. Traps: PLI-inflated margins, and revenue growth with falling RoCE.
